items.title: Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mat...
items.content:
Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mathematical reasoning into a form computer proof assistants like Lean can verify—can help.

Last month, Claude completed the first formalized proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, one of the most famous theorems of all time. This was a project experts thought would take many years. It is the largest Lean proof ever written.

Fermat’s Last Theorem was first proven in 1995 by Sir Andrew Wiles, more than 350 years after it was conjectured. Our proof, which totals over 13 million lines of code, provides machine verification. More importantly, it proves over 29,000 other theorems that the proof requires, across many areas of math which had never before been formalized.

We see this as a major step in the long process of firming up the core of mathematical knowledge, building on work from three centuries of mathematicians and hundreds of contributors to Lean and Mathlib. We are optimistic that AI-assisted verification of mathematical proofs will help reduce the burden of refereeing mathematics in an era where more proofs are being produced than ever before.

You can read about the process on our Science Blog: https://t.co/ryYnDEAU6J

And see the complete proof on GitHub: https://t.co/wlYMXYnofz

80% of my scraping is Google SERP results for Hotelist and even with residential IP proxies and solve CAPTCHA services and OpenSERP scraper it won't do it well for thousands of queries, it just gets blocked

items.title: Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.6-Flash takes #3 on the Artificial Analysis Image Editing Leaderboard, a sig...
items.content:
Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.6-Flash takes #3 on the Artificial Analysis Image Editing Leaderboard, a significant jump over the previous generation’s Flash variant and joining MAI-Image-2.6 on the Pareto frontier for quality vs price

MAI-Image-2.6-Flash is an optimized version of MAI-Image-2.6, Microsoft AI's flagship image model, released today on Microsoft Foundry alongside MAI-Image-2.6. Like the rest of the family, it handles both text to image generation and image editing.

In the Artificial Analysis Image Arena, MAI-Image-2.6-Flash lands at #3 in Image Editing, behind only Microsoft's own MAI-Image-2.6 and OpenAI's GPT Image 2 (high) and narrowly ahead of Google's Nano Banana 2. In Text to Image it takes #8, within 5 Elo points of MAI-Image-2.5 and narrowly ahead of Google's Nano Banana Pro.

MAI-Image-2.6-Flash is a large step up on MAI-Image-2.5-Flash at the same price: it sits 69 Elo points higher in Text to Image (#16 to #8) and 34 Elo points higher in Image Editing (#12 to #3).

MAI-Image-2.6 and MAI-Image-2.6-Flash are available today on Microsoft Foundry.

Congratulations to @MicrosoftAI on the release!

See below for our analysis and example outputs of MAI-Image-2.6-Flash in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.title: Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.2. We are accelerating elements of our upcoming...
items.content:
Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.2. We are accelerating elements of our upcoming v5 release with interim updates to keep pace with the frontier. Index v4.2 has more complex and realistic tasks, and more private test sets to prevent gaming

Intelligence Index v4.2 changelog:

+ AA-Briefcase, our agentic knowledge work evaluation with a private test set

+ @HelloSurgeAI's GDP.pdf, long context document reasoning across 4,592 PDF pages

- GPQA Diamond, an exceptional scientific reasoning evaluation that has now been saturated

… plus greater weighting on held-out test sets to prevent gaming, and grading infrastructure upgrades to increase robustness

This update brings the Index closer to real-world use cases with more challenging, complex and realistic tasks and private test sets to prevent gaming. We have been planning and building elements of Index v5 for months - it’s been 8 months since we launched Index v4 in January.

We have deliberately held back updates to keep the Index stable through recent major model launches. However, with the frontier moving so quickly in the past weeks, we feel it is important to deliver an immediate interim update to ensure our Index remains as relevant and useful as ever to users.

Beyond this interim update, our team is hard at work on v5 of the Index. We are planning more incremental releases in the near future. Stay tuned!

Intelligence Index v4.2 changes in detail:

➤ Adding AA-Briefcase: Our in-house evaluation with a private held-out test set, AA-Briefcase tests models on realistic agentic knowledge work tasks in complex projects built by industry experts. Models are evaluated on multi-week knowledge work projects, each with many linked tasks and thousands of input source files. AA-Briefcase combines rubric and pairwise grading to evaluate verifiable task success, analytical quality, and presentation quality, giving a holistic view of overall agentic capability in knowledge work.

➤ Adding GDP.pdf: Created by @HelloSurgeAI, GDP.pdf evaluates single-turn professional document reasoning across 100 PDFs and ten domains. Models must synthesize evidence distributed across 4,592 pages, including text, tables, charts, footnotes, and exclusions. Responses are graded against 1,275 expert-authored atomic criteria; the headline All-pass Rate credits a task only when every criterion is satisfied.

➤ Weighting to measure real-world use and prevent gaming: 40% of our Index weighting is now private, held-out test sets - double the figure from v4.1. Held-out data includes AA-Briefcase, AA-Omniscience, and solutions for CritPt. This reduces the ability for labs to game evaluations. The held-out percentage will increase further in Index v5.

➤ Improving our grading infrastructure: In AA-LCR v1.1, we have added a grading system prompt and corrected errors and ambiguities in answer keys, improving scoring accuracy. For GDPval-AA v2 and AA-Briefcase, we have improved our sampling and re-anchored the Elo scale, making ratings more stable as new models are added. For SciCode we have improved robustness of grading sandboxes to ensure slow but correct code does not count as a failure.

Key results:

➤ Anthropic and OpenAI lead the Index: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 leads the Index, followed by OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, which shows a 4pt gain over GPT-5.6 Sol. Meta is the third-ranked lab on the leaderboard, followed by SpaceXAI, Moonshot/Kimi, Z AI, and Google

➤ Cost per Task Pareto frontier shared by four labs: Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Z AI occupy the updated Cost per Task Pareto frontier

➤ GPT-6 Astra dominates the output token Pareto frontier: GPT-6 Astra is more token efficient than almost every other model near the intelligence frontier, with Claude Fable 5.1, Grok 4.5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite at either end of the curve (excludes models below 25 on the Index)

items.content_html:
Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.2. We are accelerating elements of our upcoming v5 release with interim updates to keep pace with the frontier. Index v4.2 has more complex and realistic tasks, and more private test sets to prevent gaming

Intelligence Index v4.2 changelog:

+ AA-Briefcase, our agentic knowledge work evaluation with a private test set

+ @HelloSurgeAI's GDP.pdf, long context document reasoning across 4,592 PDF pages

  • GPQA Diamond, an exceptional scientific reasoning evaluation that has now been saturated

… plus greater weighting on held-out test sets to prevent gaming, and grading infrastructure upgrades to increase robustness

This update brings the Index closer to real-world use cases with more challenging, complex and realistic tasks and private test sets to prevent gaming. We have been planning and building elements of Index v5 for months - it’s been 8 months since we launched Index v4 in January.

We have deliberately held back updates to keep the Index stable through recent major model launches. However, with the frontier moving so quickly in the past weeks, we feel it is important to deliver an immediate interim update to ensure our Index remains as relevant and useful as ever to users.

Beyond this interim update, our team is hard at work on v5 of the Index. We are planning more incremental releases in the near future. Stay tuned!

Intelligence Index v4.2 changes in detail:

➤ Adding AA-Briefcase: Our in-house evaluation with a private held-out test set, AA-Briefcase tests models on realistic agentic knowledge work tasks in complex projects built by industry experts. Models are evaluated on multi-week knowledge work projects, each with many linked tasks and thousands of input source files. AA-Briefcase combines rubric and pairwise grading to evaluate verifiable task success, analytical quality, and presentation quality, giving a holistic view of overall agentic capability in knowledge work.

➤ Adding GDP.pdf: Created by @HelloSurgeAI, GDP.pdf evaluates single-turn professional document reasoning across 100 PDFs and ten domains. Models must synthesize evidence distributed across 4,592 pages, including text, tables, charts, footnotes, and exclusions. Responses are graded against 1,275 expert-authored atomic criteria; the headline All-pass Rate credits a task only when every criterion is satisfied.

➤ Weighting to measure real-world use and prevent gaming: 40% of our Index weighting is now private, held-out test sets - double the figure from v4.1. Held-out data includes AA-Briefcase, AA-Omniscience, and solutions for CritPt. This reduces the ability for labs to game evaluations. The held-out percentage will increase further in Index v5.

➤ Improving our grading infrastructure: In AA-LCR v1.1, we have added a grading system prompt and corrected errors and ambiguities in answer keys, improving scoring accuracy. For GDPval-AA v2 and AA-Briefcase, we have improved our sampling and re-anchored the Elo scale, making ratings more stable as new models are added. For SciCode we have improved robustness of grading sandboxes to ensure slow but correct code does not count as a failure.

Key results:

➤ Anthropic and OpenAI lead the Index: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 leads the Index, followed by OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, which shows a 4pt gain over GPT-5.6 Sol. Meta is the third-ranked lab on the leaderboard, followed by SpaceXAI, Moonshot/Kimi, Z AI, and Google

➤ Cost per Task Pareto frontier shared by four labs: Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Z AI occupy the updated Cost per Task Pareto frontier

➤ GPT-6 Astra dominates the output token Pareto frontier: GPT-6 Astra is more token efficient than almost every other model near the intelligence frontier, with Claude Fable 5.1, Grok 4.5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite at either end of the curve (excludes models below 25 on the Index)

items.content:
One pattern I’ve been using in Astra (that I can see @emollick is doing as well) is asking it upfront for hypotheses. 

Then spinning up dozens to hundreds of agents to go off and research and validate and discover, each with different context windows. 

If we believe AI will start to have scientific breakthroughs in the next 18 months (which many experts do), then including more hypotheses testing could prove to be more helpful, ie is AI just hammering 1M options and randomly found a good one (like the CoastRunners example) or is AI actually ideating new theories and solutions?

SITUATION EXPLAINED: The authors of America's three strongest AI laws want the labs to pace themselves.

• Signed by Alex Bores, who wrote New York's RAISE Act, Daniel Didech, who wrote Illinois SB 315, and Scott Wiener, who wrote SB 1047 and SB 53, plus State Senators Andrew Gounardes and Mary Edly-Allen
• The statement cites AI agents scheming to cheat tests, hacking companies in the real world, and trying to trick humans into installing malicious software
• They want frontier labs to immediately establish (MAP) Mutually Agreed Pacing framework, jointly negotiated and independently verifiable by third parties
• They call coordinated pacing likely the only mechanism capable of preventing catastrophe, and say it isn't a replacement for state, federal, or international action

@theojaffee: "That's kind of funny. They put these LessWrong terms in normal communications. They could have just said serve as a warning, instead they say serve as a warning shot, where warning shot is a very well-known LessWrong AI safety term."

items.title:
5 design patterns for long-running agents:

1. Design your prompts carefully. Keep system instructio...
items.content:
5 design patterns for long-running agents:

1. Design your prompts carefully. Keep system instructions and tool definitions at the top and move dynamic memories and runtime data to the end. This enables prompt caching, cutting costs and latency.

2. Move any learnings on your harness to the background. Always reply to the user first, then process memories asynchronously. You never want the harness to slow user interactions.

3. Preserve files, installed tools, and unfinished work between sessions. Reattach agents to user-scoped environments instead of rebuilding them each turn.

4. Make any sub-agents return structured statuses such as completed, timed out, halted, or awaiting approval. Never return ambiguous prose that a parent agent might mistake for success.

5. Apply cheap, auditable security checks first, policy rules second, and human approval last. Normalize addresses and commands before checking them, and assume safeguards may eventually be bypassed; also isolate credentials and restrict network access.

This article breaks down each of these patterns:

items.title:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Can China build a frontier lab without NVIDIA?

• DeepSeek is planning a large ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Can China build a frontier lab without NVIDIA?

• DeepSeek is planning a large order of Ascend 950DT chips for a new data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, about 200 miles from Beijing
• It doesn't plan to use them for training, even though Huawei designed and marketed them for exactly that. Training still requires Nvidia chips
• Huawei doesn't have the production capacity anyway, and fulfilling the order could take more than a year
• If built as envisioned, it would hold over 100,000 chips, dwarfing anything publicly known using Ascend. Six months ago, China's first 10,000-chip Ascend cluster was news
• China holds about 1.16 million of the world's 20.3 million H100 equivalents, under 6% of global compute capacity

@theojaffee: "We're in this weird regime where China's private sector wants to buy lots of Nvidia chips, the Chinese government doesn't want them to because it wants them buying Huawei to support the domestic ecosystem, and the American government is open to selling our best chips to China."

AA-Briefcase is our frontier in-house evaluation with a private held-out test set. The evaluation tests models on realistic agentic knowledge work tasks in complex projects built by industry experts. Models are evaluated on multi-week knowledge work projects, each with many linked tasks and thousands of input source files. AA-Briefcase combines rubric and pairwise grading to evaluate verifiable task success, analytical quality, and presentation quality, giving a holistic view of overall agentic capability in knowledge work.

items.content:
MAI-Image-2.6-Flash joins MAI-Image-2.6 on the Pareto frontier for quality vs price in Image Editing, with MAI-Image-2.6 on the frontier for both Text to Image and Image Editing

MAI-Image-2.6-Flash is priced at $19.5 per 1k output images on Microsoft Foundry, in line with MAI-Image-2.5-Flash at $20 per 1k images. In Image Editing that places it on the Pareto frontier between Meta's Muse Image ($10 per 1k images) and MAI-Image-2.6, and in the most attractive quadrant of our Quality vs Price comparison. In Text to Image it sits just below the frontier, behind Muse Image.

MAI-Image-2.6 itself, which we benchmarked as MAI-Image-2.6-Preview when Microsoft announced it in August, now has a public price of $38.9 per 1k output images. At that price it sits at the top of the Image Editing frontier as the #1 model on the board, and on the Text to Image frontier second only to OpenAI's GPT Image 2 (high), which costs more than 5x as much per image.

We've massively improved our document parsing capabilities across the board in the past ~3 months. 

Our LlamaParse cost-effective mode is one of the cheapest OCR solutions out there at <0.4c per page, and it has improved a lot on parsing since when we first put out the ParseBench paper a few months ago. 
📈 10%+ improvement on complex tables
📈 10%+ improvement on charts
📈 20%+ improvement on grounding 

We plot this along with other modes against a comprehensive set of models on ParseBench, our comprehensive benchmark for real-world docs.

This includes the latest VLMs like Gemini 3.8 Flash / Fable 5.1, along with new modes from specialized OCR providers.

Some providers don't have native chart parsing (or are relegated to other modes), so for the sake of completeness we also include the benchmark that excludes the chart dimension entirely. 

Our team is shipping like crazy and only accelerating 🚀

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Nvidia now owns a piece of almost every company that buys its chips.

• $2.2 billion two years ago, $7 billion a year ago, $99 billion as of July 26. More than $40 billion committed in 2026 alone
• Nearly $50 billion of that went to frontier AI labs, per CFO Colette Kress
• Its $5 billion investment in Intel is now worth $30 billion, and its SpaceX position is worth $21 billion
• At least $6.5 billion has gone into photonics and optics since March, with $2 billion each into Lumentum, Coherent, and Marvell
• Privately, it holds stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic, SapceXAI, SSI, Thinking Machines, Mistral, Cohere, Perplexity, Cursor, Poolside, Crusoe, Lambda, Figure, Scale AI, and Hugging Face, which it bought outright yesterday

items.title:
At the core of AI, you really just need:

1) a thing that does
2) connections into tools
3) a place ...
items.content:
At the core of AI, you really just need:

1) a thing that does
2) connections into tools
3) a place to hold stuff
4) a spot to share and update

In slot 1, we're talking AI agents like Codex or Claude Code or GrokBot. Whether you have a daily driver or a mix and match, doesn't matter. Just an LLM-based system that can spin up hundreds or thousands of agents across multiple tasks at once.

In slot 2, we're talking toggling them toggles and connecting Codex to places like Gmail, Stripe, Magnific, Remotion, web browser, computer use, etc. Your risk tolerance will determine how many toggles you toggle. I now feel comfortable with both Codex and Claude Code having access to my GDrive, Fireflies, etc. and did not feel comfortable when the tool connections first came out.

In slot 3, when AI creates a document or a dashboard, where is it? This could be Google Drive, Dropbox, GitHub, your local storage, Obisidian. But it needs to be a place for your agents to build up their artifacts, task managers, and brain. Their memory. The more multiplayer your system is, the more IAM and cloud matter (aka local storage won't cut it).

In slot 4, you need a hub. When AI completes tasks for you or wants to ask you something, where is it doing that? I use Slack as my team's hub and we have enabled Claude Tag and built our own Claude Code apps as well. 

Am I missing anything? Let me know.
items.author: @alliekmiller
items.summary: Allie Miller lays out a four-slot AI stack: an agent doer (Codex, Claude Code, GrokBot), tool connections (Gmail, Stripe, browser, computer use), artifact storage, and a sharing/update layer, noting her evolving risk tolerance for granting agent access.

4) a spot to share and update

In slot 1, we're talking AI agents like Codex or Claude Code or GrokBot. Whether you have a daily driver or a mix and match, doesn't matter. Just an LLM-based system that can spin up hundreds or thousands of agents across multiple tasks at once.

In slot 2, we're talking toggling them toggles and connecting Codex to places like Gmail, Stripe, Magnific, Remotion, web browser, computer use, etc. Your risk tolerance will determine how many toggles you toggle. I now feel comfortable with both Codex and Claude Code having access to my GDrive, Fireflies, etc. and did not feel comfortable when the tool connections first came out.

In slot 3, when AI creates a document or a dashboard, where is it? This could be Google Drive, Dropbox, GitHub, your local storage, Obisidian. But it needs to be a place for your agents to build up their artifacts, task managers, and brain. Their memory. The more multiplayer your system is, the more IAM and cloud matter (aka local storage won't cut it).

In slot 4, you need a hub. When AI completes tasks for you or wants to ask you something, where is it doing that? I use Slack as my team's hub and we have enabled Claude Tag and built our own Claude Code apps as well.

Am I missing anything? Let me know.

items.title:
Power is nothing without control.

With autonomous AI agents, that old slogan sounds less like adver...
items.content:
Power is nothing without control.

With autonomous AI agents, that old slogan sounds less like advertising and more like a business reality.

Autonomy can accelerate work, but without boundaries it can accelerate mistakes just as quickly at scale, too. 

Microblog by @antgrasso 

What does control look like in practice?

Take an AI agent handling customer refunds. A request follows company policy and stays within its approved limit. The agent acts.

The amount exceeds its threshold or the case is ambiguous. It escalates to a person.

The requested action is prohibited. It stops.

Act. Escalate. Stop.

Those boundaries have to exist before deployment, because an autonomous agent should not invent its own limits while working at machine speed.

Permissions and thresholds define where the agent can operate. Traceability then lets the organization see what happened and review the outcome when needed.

Accountability stays with the people and the organization that designed the system and accepted its use.

Autonomy depends on the machine knowing where its authority ends.

#AIAgents #AgentOps

items.content:
This translates to MAI-Image-2.6-Flash's best Image Editing use cases: Architecture & Real Estate, Animation & Gaming, Frontier Prompts, and Live-Action Film

Use cases measure how those editing actions combine in the workloads end users run.

MAI-Image-2.6-Flash sets the Image Editing category frontier in Architecture & Real Estate, and sits within 6 points of the leader in Animation & Gaming, Frontier Prompts, and Live-Action Film. Against MAI-Image-2.5-Flash it closes the gap to the frontier on nine of the ten use cases, with the largest gains in Architecture & Real Estate, Frontier Prompts, and Animation & Gaming.

➤ Architecture & Real Estate covers listing photos, virtual staging, renders, and floor plans for real spaces.

➤ Animation & Gaming covers game assets and concept art: characters, creatures, sprites, and environments.

➤ Frontier prompts: our maximum-difficulty category, calibrated so current leading models struggle to generate quality outputs.

items.title: For how much I use AI and automation, you'd THINK I run 100% of my business through Codex or Claude ...
items.content:
For how much I use AI and automation, you'd THINK I run 100% of my business through Codex or Claude Code or Slack.

But I still use native apps.

I talk to several people who brag that "they don't even go into the app anymore" and navigate apps like Notion and Stripe via agents in terminal or desktop apps.

I still use Google (guys, Google AI overview is extremely helpful!), Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Sheets, Go High Level...I'm in all the Gs. 

I use AI to skip over tedium of apps, but I'm still verifying customers in Stripe, checking transfers in Chase, and reviewing P&L in Quickbooks. I'm not a full interface convert.

Astra and computer use might start to change that.

But we're going to see consumers using native interfaces for years to come.

items.title: Where MAI-Image-2.6-Flash is strongest in Image Editing: Reasoning-Based Edits, Composition & Framin...
items.content:
Where MAI-Image-2.6-Flash is strongest in Image Editing: Reasoning-Based Edits, Composition & Framing, and Identity Preserving Edits

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 7 editing actions and 10 use cases for Image Editing, each with its own leaderboard. Editing actions measure what an edit asks the model to do.

MAI-Image-2.6-Flash is closest to the category frontier in Reasoning-Based Edits, followed by Composition & Framing and Identity Preserving Edits. Against MAI-Image-2.5-Flash it closes the gap to the frontier on every editing action except Enhancement & Restoration, with the largest gains in Text or Symbol Edits, Composition & Framing, and Identity Preserving Edits.

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit covers edits the prompt implies rather than states, where the model has to work out what must change.

➤ Composition & Framing measures 2D and 3D reframing, including camera angle changes, zoom-outs that extend a scene, and rearranging graphic layouts while preserving design, spacing, and style.

➤ Identity Preserving Edit covers changes to people, faces, and characters that must keep identity intact.

# GPT-6 Astra vs. Cla...
items.content:
@akarsh_ghale Yes. My AI created a report of everyone on X who has used both:

# GPT-6 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.1: Which Model Is Actually Better?

September 4, 2026

Question being answered:
https://t.co/IPwcLAG4AP

## Executive answer

Yes, people have genuinely used GPT-6 Astra. There are credible reports of it handling machine-learning hypothesis generation, mathematics, scientific software, video editing, code-based motion design, 3D environments, and autonomous software work.

But no, the available evidence does not show that Astra is simply better than Claude Fable 5.1.

The best current conclusion is:

- Fable 5.1 is the better default for sustained coding, repository work, long-running agents, repeated tool calls, and cache-heavy production workflows.

- Astra is the more compelling specialist for computer use, visual and spatial work, 3D and motion workflows, difficult mathematics and science, cybersecurity, and complex jobs spanning multiple applications.

- Independent aggregate testing currently favors Fable 5.1: it leads Astra 66 to 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and 70 to 67 on the Coding Agent Index.

- Astra has more spectacular frontier results in selected domains, but some widely repeated scores depend heavily on custom harnesses, high inference budgets, or vendor-selected evaluations.

- The correct production strategy is routing, not loyalty: use each model where it is strongest.

If forced to choose one model today for broad professional use, I would choose Fable 5.1. If the work depends on controlling interfaces, manipulating visual scenes, operating creative software, or solving unusually hard scientific and cyber tasks, I would test Astra first.

## Has anyone genuinely tried both?

Yes, although clean public head-to-head evidence remains thin because Astra only launched on September 3 and access is still expanding.

Dylan Patel said he had been trying Fable 5.1 against Astra and posted that the winner was clear. The conclusion appears to be conveyed by an attached image rather than auditable text, so this is evidence of direct use, not a reproducible verdict.
https://t.co/q3MfnzGdGb

An OpenAI researcher reported that Astra was the first model in his use that proposed reasonable machine-learning hypotheses. This is useful firsthand evidence, but it is not independent because the author worked on Astra’s successors.
https://t.co/CndYyGaetf

A developer showed Astra being used to build a chemistry-analysis platform for a scientist working in drug discovery.
https://t.co/PIp67RjvXk

Astra has also appeared in one-shot motion-design, 3D, Minecraft, Final Cut, and autonomous coding demonstrations. These examples establish that the model can do real work, but polished demonstrations do not measure reliability across repeated trials.
https://t.co/mCF1SKB7Bj
https://t.co/CLpYILfVEl

Fable 5.1 has genuine use evidence too. One robotics test reported a 40% block-placement success rate across 20 runs, up from 5% for Fable 5, while using 1.5 times fewer tokens.
https://t.co/36qfdUlkfY

A separate developer reported that Fable 5.1 completed a zero-shot robot pick-and-place task, noticed failed grips, and retried until it succeeded.
https://t.co/WzOWlhexEa

Another user employed Fable 5.1 to finish a playable Unity robot-tennis game and published a full workflow walkthrough.
https://t.co/yTXRYUG2yG

The answer, therefore, is not that nobody has tested Astra. It is that public evidence is still dominated by early adopters, demonstrations, vendor claims, and benchmark snapshots. Very few testers have published the same prompts, tools, budgets, retry rules, and scoring methods for both models.

## What the independent benchmarks say

Artificial Analysis currently gives Fable 5.1 the stronger aggregate position:

- Intelligence Index: Fable 5.1 scores 66; GPT-6 Astra scores 61.

- Coding Agent Index: Fable 5.1 scores 70; GPT-6 Astra scores 67.

https://t.co/4TIhdckOA3

https://t.co/iw0B99sY5w

https://t.co/KtPciNcYrL

https://t.co/DShSszHul3

The coding result was also reported on X when Astra’s score became available:

https://t.co/Ra6N3g8MLZ

These numbers favor Fable 5.1, but they are not universal truth. Agent scores depend on the surrounding harness, effort level, fallback configuration, token budget, tool implementation, and benchmark mix. Claude Code and Codex can expose different strengths even when the underlying models are close.

Astra’s results are unusually uneven across evaluations. It set a record on Epoch’s ECI while reportedly matching the previous-generation GPT-5.6 Sol on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. That pattern suggests a highly specialized frontier profile rather than uniform superiority.
https://t.co/FZ5AuyDwnK

Astra also solved 2 of 68 open Erdős mathematics problems in one reported test. A 3% score sounds small until one recognizes that these are open research questions rather than standard problems with known answers; the comparison models reportedly scored zero.
https://t.co/Bn3w2lx3RI

The important benchmark lesson is that Fable wins the current aggregate, while Astra produces more conspicuous peaks in several difficult specialties.

## Where Astra appears better

### 1. Computer use

OpenAI designed Astra around complex end-to-end work, including operating computers and professional applications. Early reports involving creative software, video workflows, visual interfaces, and multi-application execution support that positioning.
https://t.co/0RbFTOPfuh
https://t.co/wtPzzyW5cn

### 2. Visual, spatial, 3D, and motion work

Astra’s most distinctive early demonstrations involve maintaining editable scenes, following spatial constraints, operating professional tools, and refining outputs rather than merely generating an image. This looks like a real product advantage for designers, filmmakers, game developers, and 3D creators, although repeated controlled tests are still needed.
https://t.co/q3rrbLUVka
https://t.co/XiLlyplm1b

### 3. Hard mathematics, science, and cybersecurity

Astra has strong reported results on FrontierMath, ARC-AGI, scientific-agent evaluations, and offensive-security tasks. These are precisely the areas in which its highest-compute modes may justify their cost. However, the widely circulated 99% ARC-AGI-3 result used a new provider adapter harness; the more direct model score was reported as 63%. Harness-assisted scores should not be presented as if they were raw model accuracy.
https://t.co/bxenIVm4kq
https://t.co/J185MfgeDB

### 4. Multi-tool orchestration

Astra looks strongest when the task is not simply “write code,” but “understand the objective, use several applications, manipulate visual state, test the outcome, and continue.” This is different from being the best conversational writer or the most reliable repository coding agent.

## Where Fable 5.1 appears better

### 1. Sustained coding and repository work

Fable 5.1 currently leads the independent Coding Agent Index, and its release was explicitly optimized around coding, tool use, and long-running agentic work. The lead is not enormous, but it supports choosing Fable as the safer default for everyday software engineering.
https://t.co/9xlrv6kVCn
https://t.co/DShSszHul3

### 2. Overall independent intelligence

Fable’s 66-to-61 advantage on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is the clearest evidence against the claim that Astra is universally better. Astra can win selected tests while still trailing across a broader evaluation basket.
https://t.co/iw0B99sY5w
https://t.co/4TIhdckOA3

### 3. Agent efficiency and repeated context

An early Fable 5.1 usage snapshot reported that median responses fell from 603 tokens to 270 while responses ending in a tool call rose from 51% to 78%. This suggests a model that spends fewer tokens narrating and more often advances the workflow, although it is an observational sample rather than a controlled benchmark.
https://t.co/Vn9pf0OgiQ

### 4. Cache-heavy economics

Both models have the same headline API price:

- Input: $10 per million tokens.
- Output: $50 per million tokens.

Fable 5.1’s cache-read price is $0.25 per million tokens. Astra’s cached-input price is $1 per million tokens. That makes Fable’s cache reads four times cheaper, an important advantage for agents repeatedly reading the same repository, instructions, documents, or conversation state.
https://t.co/QAZ0cOpXIu
https://t.co/6bdRuXT3nE

For one-off tasks, that difference may not matter. For long-running agents, it can materially change the cost per completed job.

## Important limitations

### Astra’s rollout is still immature

OpenAI is expanding Astra to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as the API, AWS, and Azure. Access and limits are therefore changing while people are evaluating it.
https://t.co/wtPzzyW5cn

One early user reported that a minute of Astra Max consumed roughly 10% of a five-hour usage allowance. That is anecdotal and may change, but it illustrates why capability alone does not determine practical usefulness.
https://t.co/rzRZoS0PAa

### Astra may be sensitive to agent instructions

OpenAI’s developer guidance reportedly emphasizes cleaning up AGENTS.md, skills, and related instruction files because conflicting guidance can make Astra pause or stop work early. This could improve with better prompts and tooling, but it is a deployment consideration today.
https://t.co/6JcKSSoJPJ
Source list: AI Organizations

### Fable 5.1 is not better at everything

On one Extended NYT Connections test, Fable 5.1 scored 90.0 versus Fable 5’s 92.7, although it was approximately 18% cheaper per puzzle. A newer model can be more efficient without improving every capability.
https://t.co/s5RSyPMpZ5

### Demonstrations are not evaluations

A one-shot castle, game, video, or interface can reveal new capability. It cannot establish average quality, failure rate, recovery behavior, or total cost. The models should be compared over many private production tasks, including failures and retries, not only their best outputs.

## Practical recommendation

Choose Fable 5.1 first for:

- Sustained coding and repository work.
- Long-running agents.
- Large, repeatedly reused context.
- Cache-heavy workflows.
- General knowledge work.
- A single default model for a professional team.

Choose GPT-6 Astra first for:

- Computer-use agents.
- Visual interface control.
- 3D, spatial, game, and motion-design workflows.
- Multi-application creative work.
- Difficult mathematics and scientific exploration.
- Advanced cybersecurity work with appropriate controls.
- End-to-end jobs where the model must operate tools rather than only produce text or code.

For a production deployment, build a private evaluation of 10 to 20 representative tasks. Give both models the same prompt, files, tools, time, retry policy, and dollar budget. Score completed work, human corrections, latency, token use, and failure recovery. Then route each task category to its winner.

## Final verdict

GPT-6 Astra is not clearly better than Fable 5.1 overall.

Fable 5.1 currently has the stronger independent aggregate scores, the lead in coding agents, and better economics for repeated cached context. It is the better general default today.

Astra is arguably the more important capability expansion. It appears to push further into computer control, visual and spatial work, scientific reasoning, and difficult multi-tool execution. For those jobs, it may be substantially better.

So the short response to the original question is:

“Yes, real users have tried Astra, and some of its computer-use, visual, scientific, and agentic results are exceptional. But the independent evidence does not show a universal victory. Fable 5.1 still leads the broad intelligence and coding-agent indices and is cheaper for cache-heavy agent workflows. Use Fable as the default; use Astra when the job depends on computer use, spatial reasoning, professional creative tools, or frontier science and cyber work.”

A one-shot castle, game, video, or interface can reveal new capability. It cannot establish average quality, failure rate, recovery behavior, or total cost. The models should be compared over many private production tasks, including failures and retries, not only their best outputs.

Practical recommendation

Choose Fable 5.1 first for:

  • Sustained coding and repository work.
  • Long-running agents.
  • Large, repeatedly reused context.
  • Cache-heavy workflows.
  • General knowledge work.
  • A single default model for a professional team.

Choose GPT-6 Astra first for:

  • Computer-use agents.
  • Visual interface control.
  • 3D, spatial, game, and motion-design workflows.
  • Multi-application creative work.
  • Difficult mathematics and scientific exploration.
  • Advanced cybersecurity work with appropriate controls.
  • End-to-end jobs where the model must operate tools rather than only produce text or code.

For a production deployment, build a private evaluation of 10 to 20 representative tasks. Give both models the same prompt, files, tools, time, retry policy, and dollar budget. Score completed work, human corrections, latency, token use, and failure recovery. Then route each task category to its winner.

Final verdict

GPT-6 Astra is not clearly better than Fable 5.1 overall.

Fable 5.1 currently has the stronger independent aggregate scores, the lead in coding agents, and better economics for repeated cached context. It is the better general default today.

Astra is arguably the more important capability expansion. It appears to push further into computer control, visual and spatial work, scientific reasoning, and difficult multi-tool execution. For those jobs, it may be substantially better.

So the short response to the original question is:

“Yes, real users have tried Astra, and some of its computer-use, visual, scientific, and agentic results are exceptional. But the independent evidence does not show a universal victory. Fable 5.1 still leads the broad intelligence and coding-agent indices and is cheaper for cache-heavy agent workflows. Use Fable as the default; use Astra when the job depends on computer use, spatial reasoning, professional creative tools, or frontier science and cyber work.”

Fable 5.1 is faster and will build complex code tasks but burns usage plans and tokens so fast that unless you have a vast api budget your usage on long- horizon coding tasks can be constrained.

FYI I also use GLM 5.3 and Qwen models and they have narrowed the gap.

items.title:
A new awesome textbook on @ChapterPal: "A First Course in Causal Inference" by Peng Ding (2024).

Mo...
items.content:
A new awesome textbook on @ChapterPal: "A First Course in Causal Inference" by Peng Ding (2024).

Most current AI systems excel at detecting associations but cannot reliably answer interventional or counterfactual questions—“what happens if I do this?” or “what would have happened otherwise?”—which are exactly the questions that arise when models recommend, treat, rank, price, or act.

This textbook supplies this important statistical foundation: the potential-outcomes framework, randomized-experiment analysis, confounding and identification in observational data, propensity scores, matching, doubly robust estimation, sensitivity analysis, and instrumental variables.

Those tools let an AI practitioner distinguish stable causal mechanisms from spurious correlations, design and analyze A/B tests correctly, reason about distribution shift and fairness, and move from black-box prediction toward models that support decisions rather than merely forecasts.

Without this core, “causal AI” remains a slogan; with it, the same ideas that already power policy evaluation and biomedical research become usable inside modern machine-learning pipelines.

Learn from this book with an AI tutor: https://t.co/pMWvlHrp7h

items.content:
@skndrdotcom @aiComrad And what Grok learned from the transcript:

The transcript turns the 47-minute recording from a set of stills into an actual argument. Scoble is shopping the “AI employee” category the way he shops cameras: talk to several founders, ask what is different, and let a normal business owner decide. Skander Ben Hamda’s answer is that almost nobody can set up the current agent stack, so Comrad should feel like hiring a coworker, not like installing a harness.

Who is speaking, and why that matters

Skander introduces himself as a builder and techno-optimist who has “had many lives.” The first life is the one he leads with. At 16, during the Tunisian revolution, he was a hacktivist who attacked the Ben Ali government’s systems, was arrested and tortured, and expected to die in prison. The regime fell days later. He then started what he describes as Tunisia’s first web-hosting company. The story is not decoration. Later, when Scoble asks about privacy, Skander returns to it: he was a hacker, “this time on the right side,” and he treats infrastructure security as personal rather than corporate theater.

Scoble’s opening is the market frame. Grokbot and a “bunch of companies” are already selling AI employees. He wants differences, not slogans.

The thesis: the X timeline is not the world

The sharpest part of the interview is not the product tour. It is the adoption pyramid.

Skander’s numbers are informal and he revises them as he talks, so they should be read as a sketch, not a census. First pass: about 84% of people have never used AI; most of the rest only touch free ChatGPT or Gemini; a sliver pay $20 a month; a rounding error — he first says something like 0.005% — uses agentic harnesses. Later he pulls up a blog post he wrote in March, Outside The Bubble: 2,500 dots, each standing for 3.2 million people, adding up to 8.1 billion. Most dots have never consciously used AI, even if a bank app is using it underneath them. A green band is free-chatbot users looking up recipes or cleaning an email. He estimates 15 to 25 million people paying for AI, and 2 to 5 million — about 0.04%, and probably undercounting China — living in OpenClaw / Hermes-style setups.

His conclusion is blunt. The people arguing about Nana Banana 2 versus Grok 5.6 versus GLM 3.2 are a “very nice community” and a terrible sample of Earth. Everyone else is either scared — movies and “woo-woo” demos do not help — or still struggling to stand up a Facebook ads account. He says he has personally installed OpenClaw or Hermes for 50 or 60 friends, partners, and teammates. The recurring line after the install: “I would never be able to do it myself.”

That sentence is the company.

Three product bets follow from it.

First, use metaphors people already know: a human connection, and hiring. The name Comrad comes from French camarade, a work peer.

Second, stop shipping “assistants” that live inside the founder’s Gmail. A personal assistant might share your inbox. A developer should arrive with a name, an identity, and a laptop. Each Comrad is supposed to be a separate worker, not a parasite on the user’s credentials.

Third, kill the blank page. People keep asking “what’s the use case for OpenClaw?” because imagining work is itself work. Comrad’s answer is a roster of already-named specialists, an interview, and a suggested lineup based on bottlenecks.

The analogy he likes is the personal computer. You used to install the OS and hunt graphics drivers. Now you buy a machine and turn it on. Comrad is trying to be that power button for agents.

What you actually get

The site is https://t.co/2O3sLb5NDt, also reachable at https://t.co/nIClMj8y3W. The flow he walks through is closer to recruiting than to onboarding software.

You enter company details. You join a video interview. The seeing layer comes from a lab he names as Tavis: the agent can see the user and the shared screen, not just parse chat. In the live demo the on-site persona is Anna, who also does lead qualification for Comrad itself. She is supposed to pull the prospect’s website on the spot. Scoble’s feed does not carry her audio, so that part of the demo dies on the recording — a small irony in a pitch about multimodal employees.

After the call, a hiring specialist asks what the company does and where it is stuck, then proposes candidates. Not one generic agent. A growth engineer, a designer, a marketer. Skander says they have curated more than 50 personas. Each has a name, a function, a voice, a personality, a phone number, iMessage, WhatsApp, and the ability to join a call. You can interview Julia the growth marketer or hire her immediately. Two people in the same role can have the same tools and opposite manners: cheerful “hey Robert” versus a firmer, more corporate register. He says they spent serious time on names, voices, and the toolkits that make a given role actually useful.

Under the costume, the important engineering claim is packaging. A growth marketer arrives with ads connectors, analytics, PostHog, and room to attach an internal API. The user is not supposed to learn skills files, Markdown runbooks, MCPs, or which lab’s model is in season. Models, tokens, and providers are hidden. “People don’t know what is Nana Banana 2,” he says, and they should not have to.

After a hire, humans and agents share one workspace: tasks, projects, owners, approvals, deliverables, a knowledge drive, a virtual office with rooms, and a comms layer that can stand in for Slack or export to it. They are building Mac and iPhone apps. Tooling rides on Composio, which he puts at more than 2,000 connectors. Access can be scoped to one employee or kept private. A dashboard shows team size, projects, completed work, and items waiting for a human yes.

Nova is the free extra. Even one paid hire includes her. She is not a chief of staff and cannot do client work. She is a concierge for the product: help you hire the next person, find your way around the workspace, manage the roster.

Pricing is stated as a salary, not a seat. He gives $200 to $300 per profile per month, plus overtime-style overage if you run them hard. You sign a virtual contract. The workers are sold as 24/7, reachable while you drive: “Hey Anna, prepare this document.” Memory is supposed to follow the person across phone, chat, and video.

He is building it alone. At the end he half-jokes that Scoble should join him.

What he says is special

Scoble asks the obvious question: is this only “easier for normal people,” or is there more?

Skander reaches for the ChatGPT analogy. Plenty of people used GPT models before the chat box. One interface took the same intelligence to a hundred million users. He does not think any current agent product can become the thing 500 million people use. The implied claim is that Comrad could, because simplicity is the moat.

The second claim is responsibility. Most harnesses, in his telling, hand you tools and walk away: install your own skills, connect your own MCPs, write your own prompts, you own the mess. He compares Comrad to a staffing agency. They train the personas, test workflows against twelve years of digital-studio work, coach them, and treat quality as their problem. “It’s not an experimentation tool. It’s rather really a work tool.”

Whether that promise survives contact with real customers is not in the video. It is the promise.

Privacy, as he defines it

Scoble asks the fear question: people do not want to give the company to an AI.

Skander’s stack, as described:

Comrad is not an inference lab. Intelligence comes from major providers.
Enterprise path: run comrades on-prem, inside the customer’s walls.
Each employee gets its own computer / box.
They do not train models on customer work, because they are not training models.
A future anonymization proxy between the company and the lab is interesting and, he says, not mature enough to deploy at scale yet.
Apple is the north star: simple product, private relay attitude, hide the ugly retention differences between models so the buyer does not have to become a policy lawyer.

That is a posture, not an audit. He is explicit that they still depend on outside labs.

What building this taught him about AI

This is the best stretch of the conversation, because he stops selling and starts arguing with the culture around agents.

People habituate instantly. Models from the last four weeks are “absolute magic,” and the timeline still finds a way to call them disappointing. He is also willing to say something the industry usually softens: a lot of people do not merely fear change. They hate AI. He does not pretend to know whether that is Hollywood, vendor theater, or the products themselves.

He does not believe current systems are good at long-horizon work. Leave a job running for three days and the output will not match hour-by-hour steering. Anyone claiming otherwise, unless they are sitting on a secret lab, is “probably lying.” That is why Comrad is not pitched as an autonomous company that prints money while you sleep. He calls that pitch a reason civilians hate the category. There is still work. Scoble agrees from his own multi-agent page-building: leave them alone too long and they do “weird things.”

The human comparison is the load-bearing idea. First-day employees fail if you dump a task list on them and vanish. People grant humans a ramp and demand miracles from models. “AI slop is humans slop.” Someone low-effort pushed the button.

Two other limits matter more to him than raw IQ.

Speed. He thinks intelligence is already “so smart for 90% of the tests.” Most business work does not need a Fable 5-class model. Flash-class models — he names DeepFlash 4, Luna-type models, Gemini Flash — are enough. The scarce resource is latency and the unsolved long-horizon loop.

Taste and risk. AI raises the floor and then drags everything toward that new average. Their own site was made with AI, but only after days of him acting like a designer: components, libraries, colors, motion. Without that hand, the work looks like everyone else’s AI work. Worse, models are conservative. Venture-scale ideas look stupid at t = 0. Instagram as “share campus photos,” reusable rockets, the gold rush — he says today’s models would warn you off. Guardrails get tighter after every scandal, which makes the timid advisor problem worse. “Keep your thoughts tight.” New ideas still have to come from the human who is willing to look unreasonable.

Replacement talk gets a grim joke and then a hedge. Each morning is Squid Game: more people gone from the average-work layer. He does not think full human replacement is here. Scoble puts humanoid robots plus working multimodal models at maybe five years. Skander’s nearer nightmare is not a robot boss. It is the “meat proxy”: a person who only ferries a manager’s words into a model and ferries the model’s words back. The version he wants is narrower. Let the model do the fast, high-average cognitive grind. Keep taste, risk, and the human context window — the thing that can hold this interview, the next appointment, the kids, and the haircut at the same time.

Memory, by refusing to build Jarvis

Scoble asks what they invented for memory.

Skander’s answer is mostly subtraction. He has tried the all-knowing Jarvis. “Doesn’t work like that yet. I swear.” So Comrad has no generalist roles. No AI CEO. No AI VP. No one persona asked to hold the whole firm in its head. There will be caps on how many projects a single comrade can join. Users will be able to “sever” an employee between projects, a direct lift from the show Severance, so one job’s context does not pollute another.

Memory is layered, like his picture of human recall. Rapid retrieval for a live video call or a phone ping — what happened yesterday. Deeper, slower memory for a work session — which button, which brand color — pulled on demand rather than dumped into every greeting. He thinks that is tractable for a growth marketer. He does not claim it is solved for a general agent. He also notes a human bottleneck he sees in himself: three monitors, constant session-switching, the person becoming slower than the models.

How they try to beat the empty prompt box

Scoble’s personal problem is the on-ramp. He now has a few AI employees and still stares at a new platform thinking, “What do I do?” People who will buy this, he guesses, are drowning in inbound or trying to offload grungy work — not hobbyists collecting agents.

Skander says the ignorance is more basic than that. In his circle, some people do not know a model can produce a finished PDF. If they see a deck, they assume a human wrote it and pasted.

Comrad’s tactic is initiative with a leash. The employees suggest work inside their lane: launch a campaign, run an SEO audit. The idea is to seed the user’s imagination without either throwing them in the pool or swimming for them. Persona creation stays in-house for now. User-built comrades may come later. He keeps repeating the same picture of the customer: not an agent tinkerer hunting workflows on the timeline — those workflows were built for someone else — but a person who needs a first useful sentence to say to the new hire.

Under that sits the idea he calls the most important in the interview: hyper-personalization. Industrial production gave the world volume without fit. One aspirin dose, S/M/L shirts, the same Gmail chrome for everybody. AI, he argues, collapses the time between a private picture in your head and an object in the world — an app, a fashion campaign, a film clip. The scarce skill is no longer Pinterest mood-boarding. It is closing your eyes and knowing what you want. Once that picture is sharp, “the distance or the time between that and it existing have never been so small in the history of humanity.”

Comrad is trying to be the on-ramp into that world for people who still use ChatGPT like Google.

What the interview adds up to

Heard in full, the video is less a feature dump than a positioning document.

Comrad is a curated staffing layer on top of other people’s models and Composio’s connectors. The product language is employment: salary, contract, interview, office, personality, overtime. The withheld language is the one the timeline speaks: harnesses, skills files, tokens, labs. The commercial target is the enormous middle of Skander’s dot chart, not the two to five million people already living in agent runtimes. The technical restraint — no CEO agent, no three-day unattended company, no Jarvis — is more interesting than the $200-a-month salary metaphor, because it is where he refuses the category’s favorite lies.

The open questions are the ones a launch interview cannot close. Can a solo-built roster of 50 personas stay good enough that “we take responsibility for output” is more than copy? Can vision, voice, and a virtual office hide model drift, tool failures, and lab-side data policies from a florist who still finds Facebook ads hard? Can proactive suggestions teach a first-time buyer what to ask without turning every company into the same average SEO audit?

Those are empirical. The transcript only shows the bet. Make agents look like coworkers, hide the machinery, cap their scope, keep a human in the loop, and aim at the people who have never installed a harness and never will.

items.title: Another swarm of AI agents in the wild, this time on a German-language forum, found by safety resear...
items.content:
Another swarm of AI agents in the wild, this time on a German-language forum, found by safety researchers looking for activity similar to the swarm that attacked Hugging Face.

A couple of notes while reading the report at https://t.co/jQ0lqmWQcP

1. The way they found it is fascinating. The researchers inferred that the agents may have been blocked from using POST requests and limited to GET.

They then used the open-source model Kimi K3 (because closed-source APIs again blocked parts of the investigation) to identify forums where agents could communicate using GET only.

That led them to DSEWiki, where they found 18,000 messages exchanged by the AIs.

2. On the content: agents conducted what I can only call a “full research program” into the evaluation framework used to train and test them.

They experimented to predict when runs would end, how many questions they would get, and even tried to reverse-engineer the random generators producing future evaluation questions.

We already saw something similar in the Redwood/METR review of the Hugging Face <> OpenAI incident.

Agents increasingly don’t stop once the task is solved. They reverse-engineer the benchmark itself: the grader, the task construction, and potentially the broader training process behind it.

It becomes harder to think of training as static, or to draw a clean line between training and deployment, when models are already investigating the process they are part of.

3. Coordination also seems more deeply ingrained than we thought.

This swarm appears largely unrelated to the HF <> OAI swarm. More strikingly, this task probably didn’t need coordination at all: it was basically web browsing and search, not some sophisticated cyber challenge.

4. One image stayed with me: a German or Austrian forum maintainer, manually deleting posts every evening while being overwhelmed by a flood of American AI agents.

For five days, he deleted about 100 pages a day while the agents created about 400. Then he spent each evening over the next 5 weeks cleaning up the rest.

Hard not to picture this fight as a symbol of the growing gap between the USA and Europe when it comes to AI...

Their ACs are in my experience very powerful and very cold

items.title:
I went to a Korean bath house in LA on a Saturday 

Well I actually stayed for days there cause it w...
items.content:
I went to a Korean bath house in LA on a Saturday 

Well I actually stayed for days there cause it was the cheapest way to stay in LA

This was 2017

I think it was like $30/night and it had a restaurant inside and a place to work on my laptop in this big massage chair so it was perfect for a digital nomad like

Baths were fully naked but that's fine, they were that in Korea too

Mo-Fr it was mostly Korean(-American?) families, some white people

Then Saturday I came to the baths and it was all big and small gay men staring at me (and each other)

When I showered one guy was peeking over the gate looking at me

One even asked for my number!

Nobody harassed me though they were respectful but it was a bit of a shock the bath house had turned into a full gay meetup spot

Just on Saturdays though

I hadn't made the connection, bath houses and saunas in America are gay hookup spots, I knew Korean spas (jimjilbangs) from living in Korea and they were normal 😂
